scenarios.title: Lift, shift, or rebuild
scenarios.situation: Your team must move a ten-year-old internal ticketing app off aging hardware in 60 days. The app is a monolith with a relational database, gets 200 users a day, and has no automated tests.
choices: Rehost it onto virtual machines as-is to hit the deadline, then plan modernization after the hardware risk is gone
Rewrite it as microservices first, then migrate, since the old code is technical debt
Refuse to migrate until full test coverage exists, to avoid carrying bugs into the cloud
Move only the database to a managed service and leave the app on the old hardware
scenarios.why: The binding constraint is the 60-day hardware deadline, not code quality. Rehosting (lift-and-shift) removes the immediate risk fastest; refactoring under a hard deadline with no tests is how migrations fail. Modernization becomes a separate, properly scoped project afterward.
scenarios.hint: Which risk kills you first: the old code or the dying hardware?

scenarios.title: Who patches the OS
scenarios.situation: Your team runs workloads two ways: virtual machines you provisioned yourself, and a managed container platform where you only deploy images. A critical OS vulnerability is announced.
scenarios.prompt: Who is responsible for patching the host OS in each case?
choices: You patch the VMs you manage; the platform provider patches the hosts under the managed container service
The cloud provider patches everything in both cases, since it is their hardware
You patch everything in both cases, since it is your application
Nobody needs to patch; the hypervisor isolates tenants from OS vulnerabilities
scenarios.why: This is the shared-responsibility model: the provider secures the infrastructure up to a boundary that moves with the service model. With self-managed VMs the OS is on your side of the line; with a managed platform the host OS moves to the provider's side, though your container images and code remain yours.
scenarios.hint: Draw the line: where does the provider's job end in each model?

scenarios.title: The egress surprise
scenarios.situation: Your cloud bill tripled this month. The compute and storage lines are flat, but data-transfer charges spiked. Your app serves large video files directly from object storage to users worldwide.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most likely cause and the durable fix?
choices: Egress charges from serving video directly from origin storage; put a CDN in front so repeat views are served from cache
The provider raised prices; open a support ticket disputing the bill
Storage grew; delete old video files to bring the bill down
A compromised key is mining crypto; rotate all keys immediately
scenarios.why: Egress (data leaving the cloud) is typically the most expensive and least intuitive line item, and serving cacheable content from origin multiplies it. A CDN caches content at edge locations, so each video traverses the paid egress path once instead of once per viewer. Disputing or deleting files treats symptoms.
scenarios.hint: Which line item moved, and what in your architecture touches it per user?

scenarios.title: One cloud or three
scenarios.situation: Leadership wants workloads spread across three cloud providers 'to avoid lock-in.' Your team is eight engineers, you have one production app, and no regulatory requirement names a specific provider.
choices: Stay on one provider and invest in portable architecture (containers, infrastructure as code) so you could move later without paying multi-cloud overhead now
Deploy to all three immediately, since lock-in is the biggest risk a startup faces
Split by tier: database on one provider, app on another, to force portability
Avoid the cloud entirely and buy servers to eliminate provider risk
scenarios.why: Multi-cloud roughly multiplies operational surface: three IAM models, three networking models, three bills, and on-call across all of them. For a small team with no regulatory driver, that cost dwarfs the theoretical lock-in risk. Portability through containers and infrastructure-as-code buys most of the exit option at a fraction of the price.
scenarios.hint: What does the second and third cloud cost you every week, not just in dollars?

scenarios.title: Commit or stay flexible
scenarios.situation: Your baseline workload runs 24/7 at steady utilization: 400 vCPUs, never dropping below 350. The provider offers ~40% off for a one-year commitment on that capacity. Finance loves the savings; engineering fears being locked in if the architecture changes.
scenarios.prompt: How should you size the commitment?
evidence:
min vCPU: 350
avg vCPU: 400
max vCPU: 620 (brief spikes)
architecture review scheduled: Q3
choices: Commit to the stable floor (around 350 vCPUs) and keep the variable headroom on flexible on-demand capacity
Commit to the full 620 peak so nothing ever runs at on-demand rates
Commit to nothing; flexibility is worth more than any discount
Commit to 400 and shut down the architecture review to protect the commitment
scenarios.why: Commitment discounts reward predictability, so you commit only the portion you are confident will still exist in a year: the floor. The burst above the floor stays elastic. Committing the peak wastes money on idle committed capacity, and committing nothing leaves guaranteed savings on the table.
scenarios.hint: Which portion of the curve are you sure about twelve months from now?

scenarios.title: The migration wave plan
scenarios.situation: You must migrate 40 services in six months. Service inventory shows deep dependencies: the auth service feeds everything, three batch jobs share one database, and nobody can diagram the full call graph.
choices: Map dependencies first, then migrate in waves starting with the least-dependent edge services and ending with shared foundations like auth
Migrate the auth service first since everything depends on it
Migrate everything in one big-bang weekend to get it over with
Migrate services alphabetically so progress is easy to report
scenarios.why: Shared foundational services are the worst first move: a failed auth migration takes down everything, including your ability to validate the migration. Starting at the edges lets the team build migration muscle on low-blast-radius services while dependency mapping reveals the safe order for the core. Big-bang maximizes correlated failure.
scenarios.hint: If the first migration fails, which choice limits the blast radius?

lessons.title: Cloud — Core concepts
concepts: Service models shift the responsibility line: with IaaS you own the OS and up; with PaaS the platform owns the runtime; with SaaS you own only your data and access. Know exactly where your side starts.
Cloud economics are opex, not capex: you trade upfront hardware spend for metered usage, which rewards elastic architectures and punishes always-on waste.
Migration has six standard strategies (rehost, replatform, repurchase, refactor, retain, retire); pick by deadline, risk, and value, not by ideology.
Multi-cloud is an operational cost, not just a negotiating tactic: every additional provider multiplies IAM, networking, billing, and on-call surface.
FinOps is a practice, not a tool: tag everything, attribute spend to owners, rightsize continuously, and match commitment discounts to your stable floor.
Design for failure across zones: regions and availability zones are the unit of resilience planning; a single-zone deployment is a single point of failure with extra steps.

example.code:
# monthly cost = hours x hourly rate (look up YOUR rate on the pricing page)
hours=730; rate=0.10   # example rate only
 echo "$hours * $rate" | bc
73.00
example.walkthrough: Every cloud cost estimate reduces to usage times unit price. Build the habit of multiplying before you deploy: one always-on instance is 730 hours a month, and small hourly rates become large annual numbers.

pitfalls: Common trap: lift-and-shift without rightsizing, which moves over-provisioned VMs into per-hour billing.
Common trap: ignoring egress; data leaving the cloud is often the most expensive line item.
Common trap: deploying with no cost tags, making the bill unattributable and therefore unfixable.
Common trap: adopting multi-cloud for leverage you will never use, while paying its complexity daily.
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

labs.title: Find the untagged spend
labs.objective: Use awk on a resource-cost CSV to total monthly spend missing cost-center tags.
steps: List all rows where cost_center is empty.
Sum monthly_usd for the untagged rows.
Compute what fraction of total spend is unattributable.
Write the three worst offending resource types to untagged-report.txt.

checks.hint: Sum the monthly_usd column only where the cost_center field is empty.
Your report should name resource types and their untagged totals.

labs.title: Rightsizing report
labs.objective: Flag chronically under-utilized instances as rightsizing candidates from utilization data.
steps: Flag instances with avg_cpu_pct below 20 as candidates.
Sum the monthly_usd of all candidates: that is your waste estimate.
Propose a smaller size class for the top three wasters and note the new estimated cost.

checks.hint: Filter rows where the CPU column is below 20 and sum their cost column.

simulations.title: The surprise bill
simulations.brief: Monday morning: last month's cloud bill is 4x the forecast. Finance is asking questions and engineering says 'nothing changed.' Find the money before the meeting at noon.

steps.symptom: The bill jumped from $12k to $48k in one month. Nobody admits to launching anything new.
evidence:
Last month: $48,210 (forecast $12,000)
Top mover: compute +$31,000 | data transfer +$4,200
Tags: 62% of spend untagged
options: Blame the forecast model and ask finance for a bigger budget
Break the bill down by service and tag, then hunt the untagged compute first
Shut down all non-production resources immediately
Open a support ticket with the cloud provider asking for a refund
steps.explain: You cannot fix what you cannot attribute. Service-by-service, tag-by-tag: the untagged 62% is where surprises live. Most 'mystery' bills are one forgotten resource type, not a pricing conspiracy.

steps.symptom: Found it: a load-test cluster from six weeks ago, still running at full size — 40 instances, untagged, in the account nobody watches.
evidence:
Resource: loadtest-cluster-07 | 40 instances x 24h x 42 days
Owner tag: (none) | Created: 6 weeks ago by ex-contractor
Cost: $30,800
options: Delete it immediately with no notice
Snapshot anything worth keeping, terminate the cluster, and notify the team first
Leave it running until the contractor confirms
Downsize it to 2 instances 'just in case'
steps.explain: Terminate, but like a professional: snapshot what might matter, tell the team before you pull the plug (someone's demo might depend on it), then kill it. 'Just in case' infrastructure is how you got a $48k bill.

steps.symptom: The cluster is gone. Now make sure this never happens again.
evidence: No more untagged, ownerless resources burning money silently
options: Mandate cost tags at creation, add a budget alert at 80% of forecast, and schedule a weekly idle-resource review
Require VP approval for every instance launch
Move everything back on-premises
Trust the team to remember next time
steps.explain: FinOps is guardrails, not gates: mandatory tags make spend attributable, budget alerts make overruns visible early, and a weekly idle-resource review makes cleanup routine. VP-approval for every VM just teaches people to work around you.

simulations.debrief: You attributed the spend, killed the zombie cluster professionally, and built guardrails instead of gates. That is FinOps: make the costs visible, then make waste impossible to ignore.

simulations.title: Lift-and-shift or re-platform?
simulations.brief: The company is migrating 60 VMs to the cloud in 90 days. The deadline is fixed; the architecture is 15 years old. Choose the migration strategy — and defend it.

steps.symptom: Sixty VMs, one 90-day deadline, a monolith nobody fully understands, and two architects arguing: 'just move them' vs 'fix them first.'
evidence:
60 VMs | monolithic app, 15 yrs old | no automated tests
Deadline: 90 days (data-center contract ends)
Team cloud experience: low
options: Re-platform everything to containers and managed services in 90 days
Lift-and-shift (rehost) now to hit the deadline, then modernize in waves after
Rewrite the application cloud-native before migrating
Delay the migration until the architecture is modern
steps.explain: The deadline is the constraint that matters: the data-center contract ends. Rehost gets you out in 90 days with the lowest risk, and modernization happens in waves once you are safe. Big-bang rewrites against fixed deadlines are how migrations die.

steps.symptom: Rehost chosen. But three VMs run a licensed database that costs 5x in the cloud under bring-your-own-license rules.
evidence:
3 VMs: commercial DB, per-core licensing
Cloud cost under BYOL: 5x current | Managed alternative: 0.4x current
Effort to switch: 3 weeks
options: Rehost them anyway — consistency beats optimization
Carve out an exception: re-platform just the database tier to the managed service
Stay on-premises for those three VMs forever
Switch database vendors entirely this week
steps.explain: Strategy is allowed to have exceptions: rehost the 57 VMs that behave, re-platform the 3 that bankrupt you. The managed database is cheaper AND removes the licensing trap. Uniformity is a means, not a goal.

steps.symptom: Migration complete. The CFO asks: 'Are we actually better off?'
evidence: CFO: 'We spent $400k migrating. Prove it was worth it.'
options: 'The data center contract ended, so we had no choice'
Show the before/after: eliminated data-center costs, deployment time from weeks to hours, and the wave-1 modernization already cut the database bill 60%
Promise savings will appear next year
Blame the licensing costs
steps.explain: Migrations are judged on outcomes, not effort: cost deltas, speed deltas, risk deltas. You measured the baseline before you moved (or you reconstructed it), and now you show the numbers. 'Trust us' is not a business case.

simulations.debrief: You let the deadline pick the strategy, made a surgical exception where the economics demanded it, and closed the loop with measured outcomes. Migration strategy is constraint management, not architecture fashion.

simulations.title: Region failover drill
simulations.brief: Game day: the primary region just 'failed' (your chaos tool killed it). Customers are hitting errors. Run the failover like it is real — because one day it will be.

steps.symptom: Health checks are red in us-east. Error rate climbing. The runbook says: declare, redirect, verify.
evidence:
us-east health: 0/12 checks passing | error rate: 34% and climbing
Runbook: 1) declare incident 2) shift DNS to us-west 3) verify
options: Follow the runbook: declare the incident, shift traffic to us-west, verify health there
Wait ten minutes to see if us-east recovers on its own
Restart everything in us-east first
Tweet that you are investigating
steps.explain: Drills exist so you do not improvise during the real thing: declare (so everyone knows), redirect (stop the bleeding), verify (trust the new region, do not assume it). Waiting 'to see' turns a drill into an outage.

steps.symptom: Traffic is in us-west. Health checks are green — but the checkout service is throwing errors for 5% of users.
evidence:
Health: 12/12 passing | checkout errors: 5%
Clue: checkout reads a cache that was only ever warmed in us-east
options: Fail back to us-east — the drill is broken
Identify the cold-cache dependency, warm it in us-west, and add cache-warming to the runbook
Accept 5% errors as the cost of failover
Blame the checkout team
steps.explain: Failover surfaced a hidden regional dependency: the cold cache. You fix it (warm it), and more importantly you write it into the runbook so the next failover does not re-learn it. Drills are for finding exactly these.

steps.symptom: All green. The drill ends. What do you do with what you learned?
evidence:
Failover time: 11 min | data loss: 0 | gap found: cold cache
Next real incident: unknown
options: File it away — the drill passed
Write the blameless postmortem: what worked, the cache gap, the runbook update, and schedule the next drill sooner
Punish whoever built the cache dependency
Declare the architecture 'multi-region ready' in the all-hands
steps.explain: A drill that finds nothing is a drill that taught nothing — yours found a real gap. The postmortem converts a lucky catch into a permanent fix, and scheduling the next drill keeps the muscle trained.

simulations.debrief: You ran the runbook instead of improvising, fixed the hidden dependency the drill exposed, and turned the lesson into process. Game days are how 'multi-region' stops being a slide and starts being a capability.

simulations.title: The open bucket
simulations.brief: A security researcher emails you: 'Your storage bucket is public. Call me.' Inside: customer exports. Work it.

steps.symptom: The researcher's screenshot shows your bucket listing customer export files, world-readable.
evidence:
Bucket: customer-exports-prod | ACL: public-read
Contents: 214 CSV exports with customer data
Researcher: 'Found via search engine. No bounty expected, just fix it.'
options: Make the bucket private immediately, then assess what was exposed
Delete the bucket and all its contents right now
Email the researcher back asking for proof first
Restrict access to the researcher's IP so they cannot see it anymore
steps.explain: Stop the bleeding first: private now. Deleting destroys the evidence you need for the exposure assessment; demanding proof wastes the researcher's goodwill while the data sits open. Private first, forensics second.

steps.symptom: Bucket is private. Now: how long was it open, and who looked?
evidence:
Bucket created 8 months ago | public since creation
Access log: 1,204 GET requests from 38 unique IPs
Your own app: 900 of those (legitimate)
options: Assume the worst quietly and say nothing
Scope it honestly: 304 non-app requests from 38 IPs over 8 months — treat as a breach, notify per policy, and document
Only count it as a breach if you can prove data was downloaded
Blame the engineer who created the bucket
steps.explain: You cannot prove a negative — 304 unexplained requests over 8 months is exposure until proven otherwise. Honest scoping, notification per your incident policy, and documentation. 'Probably nobody looked' is not a finding.

steps.symptom: Incident closed. Harden the storage posture for good.
evidence: No bucket is ever public-by-default again
options: Enable block-public-access at the account level, add a policy check to the deployment pipeline, and inventory every existing bucket
Send a reminder about bucket permissions
Move all storage on-premises
Hire someone to watch the buckets
steps.explain: Defense in depth for storage: an account-level block makes 'public' impossible by default, a pipeline check catches the drift, and the inventory finds the ones already out there. One control is a hope; three is a posture.

simulations.debrief: You closed the exposure before investigating it, scoped honestly instead of hopefully, and built three layers so it cannot recur. That is cloud security done right: fast hands, honest scope, durable guardrails.

simulations.title: The multi-cloud exit
simulations.brief: Leadership wants 'multi-cloud' to avoid lock-in. Engineering wants to go deep on one provider's managed services. The board meets Friday. Make the call.

steps.symptom: Two proposals: (A) run everything on both clouds for 'leverage'; (B) go all-in on one provider's managed services for speed.
evidence:
A: active-active multi-cloud, +60% engineering cost, portable-by-design
B: single cloud, managed services, -40% ops load, deep lock-in
Team size: 8 engineers
options: Pick A — lock-in is the bigger risk
Pick B — with 8 engineers, operational leverage beats theoretical portability
Do both: half the team on each cloud
Delay the decision until the team is bigger
steps.explain: Multi-cloud is a strategy for organizations that can afford two of everything — two skill sets, two bills, two failure modes. With 8 engineers, the real risk is not lock-in, it is drowning in undifferentiated operations. Go deep, ship fast, revisit at 10x scale.

steps.symptom: Single cloud chosen. Now address the lock-in fear without building a second cloud.
options: Keep all infrastructure as code, use open interfaces at the boundaries, and keep the data exportable — portability without a second cloud
Build a shadow deployment on the other cloud just in case
Negotiate a price lock and stop worrying
Accept the lock-in as the cost of doing business
steps.explain: The cheap version of multi-cloud is exit-readiness: everything as code, open interfaces, exportable data, and a tested restore somewhere else. You do not need two clouds running — you need one cloud you could leave.

steps.symptom: Friday board meeting. One slide to defend the decision.
evidence: Board: 'Why not multi-cloud like our competitors?'
options: 'Because our competitors are bigger than us'

'Active-active multi-cloud costs us 60% more engineering for insurance we cannot collect: with our team size we would run both clouds badly. Instead we are exit-ready — portable code, exportable data, tested restores — at a fraction of the cost.'
'We will revisit it next year'
'The engineers prefer one cloud'
steps.explain: Decisions presented as trade-offs with numbers survive board meetings; preferences do not. You named the cost of the alternative, the risk of the chosen path, and the mitigation — that is a strategy, not a preference.

simulations.debrief: You sized the strategy to the team, bought exit-readiness instead of a second cloud, and defended it with economics. Multi-cloud is a means; the goal is leverage without fragility.

consoleSims.title: Build the landing zone network
consoleSims.brief: Every cloud migration starts with the network. Create a VPC named lab-vpc (10.1.0.0/16), then carve a public subnet 10.1.1.0/24 in us-east-1a inside it.

tasks.instruction: Create a VPC named lab-vpc with CIDR 10.1.0.0/16.
tasks.hint: Open the VPC section and create a VPC: NAME=lab-vpc, CIDR=10.1.0.0/16.

tasks.instruction: Create a subnet 10.1.1.0/24 in lab-vpc, availability zone us-east-1a.
tasks.hint: Create a subnet inside lab-vpc: VPC=lab-vpc, CIDR=10.1.1.0/24, AZ=us-east-1a.

consoleSims.debrief: Network first, everything else second. A VPC with a real subnet is the foundation every workload after this will stand on.

consoleSims.title: Lock down the web tier
consoleSims.brief: The web tier needs a security group that allows HTTPS from anywhere — and nothing else. Create the group web-sg on a VPC, then add the single inbound rule.

tasks.instruction: Create a VPC named web-vpc with CIDR 10.3.0.0/16 (the group needs a home).
tasks.hint: Create a VPC first: NAME=web-vpc, CIDR=10.3.0.0/16.

tasks.instruction: Create a security group named web-sg on web-vpc.
tasks.hint: Create a security group: VPC=web-vpc, NAME=web-sg.

tasks.instruction: Add an inbound rule to web-sg: TCP port 443 from 0.0.0.0/0.
tasks.hint: Add an inbound rule on web-sg: PROTOCOL=tcp, PORT=443, CIDR=0.0.0.0/0.

consoleSims.debrief: Security groups are whitelists: one explicit allow, everything else denied. The web tier gets exactly HTTPS and nothing more.

consoleSims.title: Onboard the deploy bot
consoleSims.brief: Automation needs an identity too. Create a user named deploy-bot for the CI system, then enable MFA on it — bots get the same identity hygiene as humans.

tasks.hint: Open Users and create a user: NAME=deploy-bot.
Enable MFA on the deploy-bot user — find the MFA action on the user row.

consoleSims.debrief: Every identity — human or machine — gets MFA. The deploy bot is one of the most powerful accounts you own; protect it like one.

consoleSims.title: Stand up the migration resource group
consoleSims.brief: The migration's second region lives in Azure. Create a resource group migration-rg in eastus, then a virtual network 10.2.0.0/16 inside it.

tasks.instruction: Create a resource group named migration-rg in location eastus.
tasks.hint: Create a resource group: NAME=migration-rg, LOCATION=eastus.

tasks.instruction: Create a virtual network with CIDR 10.2.0.0/16 in migration-rg.

consoleSims.debrief: Resource groups are the unit of lifecycle: everything for the migration lives, gets tagged, and can be deleted together. Multi-cloud starts with tidy foundations.

terminalMissions.title: Name your region
terminalMissions.brief: Every cloud resource lives in a region. Print this machine's hostname — its region codename for this drill.
terminalMissions.success_message: Region named. Resources without regions are just hopes.

terminalMissions.title: Who is deploying
terminalMissions.brief: Deployments are attributed to identities. Print your username.
terminalMissions.success_message: Deployer identified. Every change has an owner.

terminalMissions.title: List the migration staging area
terminalMissions.brief: Before migrating anything, map the territory. List the home directory.

checks.hint: Run: ls — map the staging area.

terminalMissions.success_message: Territory mapped. Migrations fail when people move things they never inventoried.

terminalMissions.title: Confirm the working directory
terminalMissions.brief: Cloud consoles are context-sensitive — the wrong directory means the wrong deployment. Print yours.
terminalMissions.success_message: Context confirmed. Deploy from the wrong directory and you deploy the wrong thing.

terminalMissions.title: State the migration wave
terminalMissions.brief: Migrations move in waves. Announce the current wave with echo — status must be stated, not assumed.

checks.hint: Run: echo with the wave status (e.g. echo "wave 1 complete").

terminalMissions.success_message: Wave stated. Silent migrations are how cutovers surprise people.

terminalMissions.title: Verify the platform
terminalMissions.brief: Instance types matter. Print the full system information to confirm the platform architecture.
terminalMissions.success_message: Platform verified. Right-size from facts, not guesses.

terminalMissions.title: Attest the deploy identity
terminalMissions.brief: Print your full identity record, then attest it with echo — the deploy bot gets the same identity hygiene as humans.

checks.hint: Run: id — read the full identity string.
Run: echo with an attestation (e.g. echo "identity attested").

terminalMissions.success_message: Identity attested. Every deploy identity — human or machine — gets verified.

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about the most technically difficult problem you have run into — a homelab, a broken environment, anything — and how you solved it.
points: Pick ONE problem with a real evidence trail: the symptom, what you measured, the hypothesis you tested
Show the loop: scope, observe, hypothesize, smallest safe change, validate — interviewers score the method, not just the fix
Name the tools (VM build, networking, logs) and the lesson it taught you
Close with the result in concrete terms: what works now that did not before
pitfalls: Choosing a story with no real obstacle (“I Googled it” is not a story)
Skipping validation — saying it worked without proving it
Rambling past two minutes without reaching the result

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you dealt with a frustrated customer or user while something was broken.
points: Lead with empathy and ownership: acknowledge the impact before the technical detail
Show translation: what you told them, in their language, plus the timeline you committed to
Show judgment: the narrow fix you chose and what you refused to do (e.g., disabling the control to clear the symptom)
Close with the relationship outcome, not just the technical one
pitfalls: Badmouthing the customer to sound decisive
Promising a timeline you could not keep
Framing the user as the problem rather than the situation

points: Connect prevention to something concrete: a moment you saw detection arrive too late, or a system you hardened
Tie their model to your instincts: deny-by-default matches how you already think about trust
Show service orientation: the Cyber Hero culture rewards the 2 a.m. helper — give an example of being one
Name one forward-looking reason: Zero Trust, the MSP mission, or the bootcamp community investment
pitfalls: Generic flattery with no specifics about the company
Leading with compensation, title, or location convenience
Claiming expertise in products you have only read about — frame it as studied, not mastered
Staying vague ('I analyzed the data') instead of naming what you connected.
Skipping your own role: what did YOU see that others missed?
No outcome: what changed because you joined the dots?
points: The scattered signals and why nobody had connected them yet
The specific links you drew between them (shared host, time, infrastructure)
What the bigger picture turned out to be and what action it drove
What the experience taught you about investigating
behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you connected scattered clues into a bigger picture that others had missed.

pitfalls: Claiming you fixed everything: credibility comes from trade-offs, not heroics.
Hiding the constraint: the limitation is what makes the prioritization story real.
No metric: 'better' needs a before-and-after.
points: The constraint (time, budget, staff) and the size of the backlog
How you decided what mattered most (what was reachable, what was critical)
What you did first and what you deliberately deferred
The measurable result of the prioritization
behavioral.prompt: Describe a time you had to prioritize risks or fixes with limited time or resources. How did you decide what came first?

pitfalls: Reciting jargon to a non-technical audience and calling it communication.
Skipping the audience's reaction: did they actually understand and act?
Making yourself the hero instead of the translator.
points: The technical finding and why it mattered
Who the audience was and what they cared about
How you reframed it (a picture, an analogy, a story)
What decision or action the audience took because they understood
behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you explained a complex technical finding to a non-technical audience and it changed a decision.
Tell me about a time you used automation or AI to solve a security problem.
points: The repetitive security task and what it cost in analyst time
The automation or AI approach you built and how you validated it
Measured outcome: time saved, detection gained, false positives changed
pitfalls: Describing the tool but never the validation
No measurable outcome

behavioral.prompt: Describe a time you had to decide whether to trust an automated security decision.
points: The stakes of the automated action and its blast radius
How you verified before acting (or the gate you built)
What happened and what you would automate differently next time
pitfalls: Saying you always trust the tool
No mention of blast radius or reversibility

sections.heading: Company facts (verified)
items: Founded 2017 in Orlando, FL — Danny Jenkins (CEO), Sami Jenkins (COO), John Carolan (QA)
Philosophy: deny-by-default / default-deny — approve known-good, deny the rest
Customers: 70,000+ organizations, sold heavily through the MSP channel
Funding: $190M Series F, July 2026 (Elephant-led); ~730 employees
Interview address: 1901 Summit Tower Blvd, Orlando, FL 32810
Culture: in-office 5 days/week; free lunch; post-offer background + drug screening

sections.heading: Product stack
items: Allowlisting — default-deny execution control for apps, DLLs, scripts, installers
Ringfencing — constrains allowed apps: app-to-app, file, registry, network
Storage Control — USB/device policy by serial, user, file type, encryption
Elevation Control — just-in-time per-app admin, no standing rights
Network Control — host firewall; port/IP/dynamic-ACL rules; ZTNA foundation
Web Control — agent-based DNS/URL category filtering, works off-network
Cyber Hero MDR — 24/7/365 US-based response, ~60-second average
Testing Environment — one-button VDI sandbox; checks AV flags, canary files, registry changes

sections.heading: Rule strength (strongest to weakest)
items: Certificate/publisher rules — survive version updates
Hash rules — precise but break on every new version
Path rules — weakest; never in user-writable locations
Learning Mode catalogs before enforcement; Installation Mode pauses blocking — scope and time-box both

sections.heading: Terminal evidence commands
items: nmap <host> — which ports answer (22/80/443 open)
dig <name> — ANSWER SECTION with the A record
ss — listening sockets
systemctl status <svc> — unit state
journalctl -u <svc> — service logs
sha256sum <file> — real SHA-256 identity
grep <pattern> <file> — search the record
ps — what is actually running

sections.heading: Graph vocabulary
items: node — any entity tracked in the model (user, host, IP, domain, file hash, vulnerability)
edge — a labeled relationship between two nodes (logged into, resolved to, downloaded)
degree — number of edges on a node; high-degree nodes are attacker highways
centrality — how much traffic or how many paths flow through a node
directed edge — a relationship with a direction (A downloaded FROM B)
security graph — the living model of your whole environment as nodes and edges
attack graph — the subgraph of exploitable paths to your targets
knowledge graph — threat-intel indicators linked to campaigns and actors

sections.heading: Attack-graph playbook
items: inventory first — you cannot graph what you have not discovered
model flaws AND misconfigs as exploit edges
compute shortest paths to the crown jewels
find the choke point (highest betweenness on those paths)
break the path: patch, segment, or remove the edge
re-scan and re-run the graph to prove the path is gone
never trust yesterday's graph — redeployments redraw the map

sections.heading: Zero Trust + graphs
items: never trust, always verify — re-evaluate every access decision
assume breach — treat unexpected edges as hostile until proven otherwise
microsegmentation — allow-list approved edges, alert on new ones
ReBAC — policies are path queries on the identity graph
continuous verification — device/location/behavior edges change, trust follows
anomalous edge — a first-seen connection between strangers is the classic signal

sections.heading: ML detection vocabulary
items: Supervised learning — learns from labeled examples; strong on known threats, blind to novel ones
Unsupervised learning — finds structure without labels; clustering and dimensionality reduction
Anomaly detection — models 'normal' and flags deviations; the workhorse for novel threats
UEBA — user and entity behavior analytics: per-user baselines plus peer-group comparison
Feature engineering — encoding raw logs into model inputs (login velocity, rare processes, domain entropy)
Concept drift — model decay as attacker behavior and legitimate traffic shift over time

sections.heading: Detection metrics
items: Precision — of all flagged alerts, how many were real
Recall — of all real attacks, how many were flagged
Threshold tuning — sliding the decision cutoff trades precision against recall
Alert fatigue — when false positives train analysts to ignore the queue
DGA — domain generation algorithm; detected via character entropy of domain names

sections.heading: Agent and LLM security
items: Direct prompt injection — attacker input overrides app instructions (OWASP LLM01:2025, the #1 LLM risk)
Indirect prompt injection — hidden instructions inside retrieved data (email, web, docs)
Jailbreak — defeating the model's own safety policy; distinct from hijacking app behavior
Tool poisoning — malicious tool descriptions or metadata steer an agent to misuse its tools (MCP ecosystem risk)
Insecure output handling — executing or trusting model output without validation
Least-privilege tools — grant each tool only the scope its task requires

sections.heading: Adversarial ML and governance
items: Evasion — perturbing inputs at inference time to dodge a classifier
Poisoning — corrupting training data to corrupt the model
Extraction — querying a model to steal its behavior or parameters
MITRE ATLAS — knowledge base of adversarial ML tactics and techniques
Red-teaming and evals — adversarial testing of AI systems before deployment
Human-in-the-loop — required approval for high-impact or irreversible agent actions
SOAR — security orchestration, automation and response; automate enrichment, gate containment

glossary.def: Default-deny execution control: only explicitly approved applications, scripts, and installers may run.
Default-allow model: everything runs except recognized-bad items — the window zero-days live in.
Deny-by-default posture: unknown code, devices, or connections are refused unless explicitly approved.
Containment applied on top of allowlisting; restricts what a permitted app may do across app-to-app, file, registry, and network dimensions.
Agent mode that catalogs applications and dependencies and auto-builds policies before enforcement; temporarily disables file blocking.
Temporary mode that pauses file blocking for installs — must be tightly scoped and time-boxed.
Grants specific approved applications admin rights for standard users — just-in-time, per-app, time-boxed — without standing admin rights.
An elevated or trusted process spawning another tool (e.g., PowerShell) to inherit its privileges — countered by ringfencing the elevated process.
Device and path policy: USB approved by serial, user, file type, time, and encryption; unapproved devices do not connect.
Centrally managed host firewall; rules by port, source IP, and dynamic ACLs; egress allowlisting pins apps to approved destinations.
Zero Trust Network Access: per-session, per-application brokered connections (commonly over port 443) with no open inbound ports — deny-by-default for network access.
Portal queue where end-user software requests arrive for admin review and decision.
Real-time audit showing what was allowed or denied across endpoints — and why; the evidence layer for triage.
One-button cloud VDI sandbox launched from an approval request; logs AV flags, canary-file access, and registry/system changes.
24/7/365 US-based managed detection and response team; validates alerts, isolates hosts, acts on customer runbooks; ~60-second average response.
Design and operate as if the attacker already has a foothold — least privilege, containment, and monitoring everywhere.
Attacks that hijack trusted built-in tools (Word, PowerShell) instead of dropping malware — defeated by behavior containment, not signatures.
Scoped, ticketed, tested changes with validation and rollback — emergency speed never cancels the process.
A node in an attack graph representing a system or weakness, connected by edges that represent steps an attacker could take between them.
How central a node is to paths through the graph (for example, betweenness: how many shortest paths cross it).
The most valuable assets in the environment (customer data, finance systems, source code): what attack paths are measured against.
A labeled connection between two nodes, representing a relationship such as 'logged into' or 'resolved to'.
A graph of threat indicators (IPs, domains, hashes) linked to campaigns, actors, and each other through shared infrastructure.
The practice of mapping relationships in data to reveal hidden associations; rooted in Euler's 1736 graph theory, 1970s paper link charts, and post-2001 intelligence work.
A segment of the network so small that its allowed communications can be enumerated as a graph of approved edges.
An entity in the graph: a user, host, IP address, domain, file, or vulnerability.
Access control where policy is evaluated by traversing relationships on a graph (for example: user reports_to manager who owns the resource's project).
A machine-learning model that operates directly on graph structure to classify nodes or subgraphs, for example labeling attack vs normal behavior.
Monitoring user and entity behavior by modeling their normal relationship patterns and flagging structural anomalies.
ML trained on labeled examples; classifies new inputs into known categories.
ML approach that models normal behavior and flags statistically rare deviations.
Turning raw telemetry into numeric model inputs, e.g. login velocity or domain entropy.
Share of flagged alerts that were real; the false-positive economics of the queue.
Share of real attacks the detector flagged; the miss rate's complement.
Decay of model performance as the data distribution shifts over time.
Attacker-crafted instructions that override an LLM application's intended behavior; direct (user input) or indirect (retrieved data).
Crafted input that defeats an LLM's own safety policy or refusal behavior.
Malicious tool descriptions or metadata that manipulate an AI agent into misusing its tools.
Failing to validate LLM output before acting on it, e.g. executing generated commands.
Adversarial ML technique: perturbing inputs to cross a classifier's decision boundary.
Adversarial Threat Landscape for AI Systems; MITRE's knowledge base of AI attack tactics.
Security orchestration, automation and response; playbooks that enrich automatically and gate containment on humans.
Required human approval before high-impact or irreversible automated actions.

checklist: Sixty-second company brief rehearsed out loud: year, city, philosophy, three products, one milestone
Two STAR stories ready: hardest technical problem; a frustrated customer or user
“Why ThreatLocker / why cybersecurity” answer tied to prevention and service, not slogans
Ringfencing explained in one plain-English sentence (the Word-on-a-leash version)
Elevation Control answer ready: just-in-time, per-app, time-boxed, ringfenced, logged
Triage loop memorized: scope → observe → hypothesize → smallest safe change → validate → explain
Three questions to ask them: team on-call shape, approval SLA expectations, what “most helpful” looks like on the team
Logistics: 1901 Summit Tower Blvd, Orlando FL; in-office role; ID and references ready
Define your crown jewels before you model anything.
Build the asset-and-access graph from live sources (scans, configs, identity), not from the CMDB alone.
Model vulnerabilities AND misconfigurations as exploit edges.
Compute shortest attack paths to each crown jewel; name the choke points.
Prioritize remediation by path risk, not by raw severity score.
Express at least one access policy as a relationship path (ReBAC pilot).
Baseline approved communication edges per segment; alert on first-seen edges.
Brief the next incident or risk review with the graph, not a spreadsheet.
Can you explain supervised vs unsupervised vs anomaly detection with a security example for each?
Can you name three log features you would engineer for a C2 detector and why?
Can you walk through a UEBA alert (baseline, deviation, verification) end to end?
Can you explain the precision/recall tradeoff and how you would set a threshold for a fatigued SOC?
Can you define concept drift and describe a retraining process?
Can you distinguish direct vs indirect prompt injection and jailbreaking?
Can you explain tool poisoning in the MCP ecosystem and three controls against it?
Can you describe insecure output handling and how you would validate agent output?
Can you name the three adversarial ML attack classes and one defense for evasion?
Can you design a SOAR playbook gate: what automates freely, what needs human approval?

media.title: Allowlisting vs blocklisting: default-deny vs default-allow
media.caption: Default-deny stops unknown code without a signature; default-allow runs it until one exists.
media.alt: Side-by-side comparison: on the left, a default-deny gate runs known-good payroll software and denies unknown ransomware with no signature needed; on the right, a default-allow gate runs both until the ransomware is recognized as bad.

media.title: Ringfencing: four leashes on an allowed application
media.caption: Word stays approved, but it cannot spawn PowerShell, read the credential store, or reach the internet — while opening its document is allowed.
media.alt: An approved Word application inside a dashed containment ring: arrows show PowerShell launch denied, credential-store registry access denied, external network denied, and document file access allowed.

media.title: The Zero Trust endpoint stack
media.caption: Five deny-by-default layers — Allowlisting, Ringfencing, Elevation, Storage, Network — watched by Web Control, the Testing Environment, Unified Audit, and the Cyber Hero MDR team.
media.alt: A vertical stack of five layers from Allowlisting at the foundation up through Ringfencing, Elevation Control, Storage Control, and Network Control, with side boxes for Web Control, Testing Environment, Unified Audit, and Cyber Hero MDR.

media.title: Application-request triage flow
media.caption: Gather evidence first, then branch: trusted gets a scoped rule, unknown goes to the sandbox, malicious gets a documented deny.
media.alt: Flowchart from request arrival through evidence gathering to a decision diamond branching into three outcomes: approve with a scoped rule, detonate in the Testing Environment then ringfence, or deny with documented evidence.
Diagram of four labeled nodes (user, host, file, domain, IP) joined by labeled directed edges such as logged into, downloaded, and resolved to, illustrating graph vocabulary.
media.caption: Nodes are the things; edges are the relationships. Attackers move along the edges.
media.title: Graph vocabulary: nodes and edges

media.alt: Attack graph with four nodes in a chain: external attacker to VPN gateway to file server to customer database, with a dead-end branch to a printer, showing the shortest path to the crown jewel.
media.caption: The shortest path to the crown jewel is length 3. Break the choke point and the campaign dies.
media.title: Attack graph: shortest path to the crown jewels

media.alt: Seven kill-chain stages as connected graph nodes: reconnaissance, weaponization, delivery, exploitation, installation, command and control, actions. Three alerts are annotated at delivery, installation, and command and control.
media.caption: Three 'unrelated' alerts, one kill-chain subgraph. Correlate by shared entities, not by severity.
media.title: Kill chain as a graph

media.alt: A policy engine at the center of a small graph evaluates an access request from a finance user on an untrusted laptop to an R and D code server. The request is denied because there is no prior relationship edge and the device is untrusted.
media.caption: Valid credentials are not enough. The graph checks device trust, history, and relationships on every request.
media.title: Zero Trust runs on relationships
ML detection pipeline: telemetry to triage
media.caption: How raw telemetry becomes scored alerts: features feed the model, the model scores, analysts triage top-down — and analyst verdicts feed retraining.
media.alt: Flow diagram: telemetry sources feed feature extraction, which feeds an ML model, which outputs scored alerts into an analyst triage queue, with a feedback arrow for retraining.

media.title: UEBA: baseline vs deviation
media.caption: UEBA learns each user's normal hours, locations, and volumes, then scores deviations from that baseline.
media.alt: 24-hour timeline showing a shaded normal login window from 8 AM to 6 PM with normal logins inside it, and a red anomaly marker at 2:47 AM for a foreign login scoring 97 out of 100.

media.title: Indirect prompt injection attack flow
media.caption: An attacker hides instructions in data the agent retrieves; the agent mistakes data for instructions and misuses its tools.
media.alt: Attack flow diagram: hidden instruction in an email is read by an AI agent, which mistakes it for a command and calls a privileged tool, causing fraud; three defense boxes below: sanitize content, least-privilege tools, human approval.
